strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: extends the rationalist vs. empiricist discussion in causal inference by proposing an unsupervised, data-driven pipeline (FM + SAE + hypothesis testing) for discovering treatment effects in high-dimensional data, rather than requiring the outcome variable(s) to be known/labeled a priori.

Identifies and formally characterizes a genuine and underappreciated statistical pathology (the 'paradox of exploratory causal inference'): as sample size or effect magnitude grows, standard multiple-testing correction fails to control for entangled/leaked neurons, and the paper backs this up with clean asymptotic theorems (3.1, 3.2) and a clear numerical illustration.

The proposed Neural Effect Search (NES) algorithm is a reasonably elegant fix (recursive stratification + residualization) with an accompanying consistency theorem and detailed, honest proof sketches/assumptions in the appendix (sufficiency, alignment, arm-wise decomposition with bounded leakage).

Reasonably thorough empirical validation: a controlled semi-synthetic CelebA benchmark with known ground truth (varying n and effect size, r known/unknown regimes), plus a real-world randomized trial (ISTAnt ecology dataset) where the method recovers a previously known effect (grooming) in a purely unsupervised way, lending some real-world credibility.

Extensive appendix ablations (zero-effect sanity check, choice of per-round test, AIPW vs. associational difference) that probe robustness and calibrate expectations about when NES is preferable to simpler procedures.
Reproducibility efforts are reasonable: code snippet included, promise of full code release, detailed experimental protocol in the appendix.
Clear, honest limitations/discussion section acknowledging the central untested assumption (identifiability/monosemanticity of SAEs) rather than overselling the method.
weaknesses: The real-world validation is very thin: n=44 videos, and NES surfaces only two neurons, one of which merely reproduces an effect already known and manually annotated in prior work (grooming) and the other is a somewhat trivial background/design artifact. There is no case where the method uncovers a genuinely new, previously unknown scientific effect, which is the paper's central motivating promise ('discover the unknown effects of a treatment'). The quantitative validation of the second neuron is also absent (only qualitative judgment is given).

The method's soundness rests on strong, largely unverifiable assumptions in real applications: FM sufficiency (I(X,Y)=I(φ(X),Y)), (approximate) SAE monosemanticity/linear representation hypothesis, and the 'good identifiability' assumption that the authors themselves flag as their weakest premise. Given the cited negative literature on SAE faithfulness (Heap et al., Leask et al., Chanin et al., Wu et al.), it is unclear how much the theoretical guarantees (Theorem 4.1 and its many sub-assumptions A.1-A.3) transfer to practice beyond curated synthetic benchmarks.

The semi-synthetic benchmark, while useful, is fairly narrow (r=2 CelebA attributes, single confounder W), and it is unclear how NES performance degrades with more effects, more entanglement, or continuous/non-binary outcomes (explicitly out of scope here).

Baselines are limited to generic multiple-testing corrections (Bonferroni, FDR, t-test, top-k); no comparison to other SAE-based scientific discovery methods mentioned in the related work (e.g., HypotheSAEs) or to alternative disentanglement/causal representation learning approaches, making it hard to gauge NES's relative advantage against more specialized competitors.

Practical guidance on hyperparameters (ε threshold for leakage, stratification bin granularity, when to relax/skip Bonferroni) is somewhat ad hoc and decided per-experiment (e.g., dropping Bonferroni entirely for the small real-world trial), raising questions about how a practitioner would choose these in a genuinely novel exploratory setting without ground truth to tune against.

Heavy reliance on and overlap with the authors' own prior work (Cadei et al. 2024, 2025) for both the real dataset and the motivating narrative, which slightly limits the independence of the real-world validation and the novelty framing relative to that prior line of work.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: bridging exploratory/data-driven hypothesis generation with formal causal inference, addressing the real 'Matthew effect' limitation of rationalist RCT analysis.

Clear theoretical contribution: formal identification and proof of the 'Paradox of Exploratory Causal Inference' (significance collapse under increasing power/sample size), and a consistency theorem for the proposed Neural Effect Search (NES) algorithm under explicit, if strong, assumptions.

Very extensive empirical validation in the appendix: ablations over foundation model choice (SigLIP vs DINOv2), SAE dimension, non-linearity (top-k vs JumpReLU), random seeds, hypothesis-testing variant (Bonferroni/FDR/t-test), residualization, ATE estimator (AD vs AIPW), varying DGPs (opposite effects, unbalanced propensity, zero-effect sanity check), and two additional CFL-inspired baselines — all consistently supporting the core claims.

Demonstration on a genuine real-world scientific trial (ISTAnt ants dataset) with qualitative interpretation validated against biologist judgment and quantitative F1 agreement with previously manually annotated behavior (grooming), plus a sensible interpretation of a spurious experimental-design artifact.

Good positioning relative to related work (CFL, causal representation learning, HypotheSAEs), clearly articulating what is novel (statistical significance testing for causal outcome discovery rather than mere correlation-based hypothesis surfacing).
Reasonable reproducibility effort: public datasets, detailed appendix experimental protocols, and a minimal Python implementation snippet.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees hinge on several strong and practically untestable assumptions (sufficiency of V, principal alignment/margin conditions, bounded leakage ε, near-monosemantic SAE codes) that the paper's own ablations show can be violated (e.g., JumpReLU SAEs fail principal alignment), meaning the method's validity in a genuinely 'exploratory' setting (without ground-truth labels to check assumptions) cannot be verified a priori.

The real-world case study is a single, small-scale demonstration (n=44 videos, only 2 discovered neurons) that essentially re-confirms an already-known effect (grooming, previously identified via the rationalist/annotated approach) plus a background-marking confound — it does not clearly demonstrate discovery of a genuinely novel, previously unknown scientific effect, which is the paper's central motivating promise.

Practical usability depends on numerous hyperparameters (top-k sparsity level, SAE latent dimension, non-linearity type, stratification binning, significance threshold) whose selection is not principled and is only justified post-hoc through extensive ablations rather than a priori guidance for a practitioner facing a truly unknown effect.
The method is restricted to discrete/binary outcomes; continuous outcome concepts are explicitly out of scope, limiting generality for many real scientific applications.

The semi-synthetic evaluation, while extensive, is limited to a small number of known ground-truth effects (r=2) and relatively simple co-effect structures; scalability and behavior with many simultaneous/weaker effects (more realistic exploratory scenarios) is not well characterized.

The paper is dense and heavily theory-laden in the main text, deferring most empirical substance to a very large appendix, which may reduce accessibility and makes it harder to assess the core claims from the main paper alone.

strengths: Novel and interesting problem framing at the intersection of causal inference, foundation model representations, and SAE-based interpretability, addressing a real gap: how to generate data-driven causal hypotheses without a priori labeling.

Solid theoretical development: the paper formally characterizes the 'paradox of exploratory causal inference' (multiple-testing collapse under entanglement) and proves consistency of the proposed Neural Effect Search algorithm under stated assumptions.

Extensive robustness checks in the appendix: variations across foundation models (SigLIP, DINOv2), SAE dimensionality, non-linearities (top-k vs JumpReLU), random seeds, hyperparameters (residualization, hypothesis test type, ATE estimator), and structural causal model variants (opposite effects, unbalanced propensity, zero-effect sanity check).
Reasonably good reproducibility: pseudocode, a minimal Python implementation snippet, and detailed experimental settings are provided.
Honest and thorough limitations/ethics discussion, explicitly flagging identifiability concerns and cautioning against over-interpreting the method's outputs without domain expert validation.
weaknesses: The central empirical validation on a genuinely 'unknown' real-world scientific discovery is weak: the ISTAnt experiment uses only n=44 videos and NES returns just two neurons. One (grooming) simply re-confirms an already known effect from prior work by the same authors, and the other is an experimental design artifact (background marking confound), not a novel biological discovery. This undercuts the paper's headline claim of being 'the first successful unsupervised causal effect identification on a real-world scientific trial,' since no genuinely novel, previously-unknown effect is demonstrated.

The quantitative fidelity of the real-world discoveries is modest (F1=0.398 and F1=0.568 against expert-annotated behaviors), which is not strong evidence that the discovered neurons cleanly correspond to interpretable, scientifically meaningful concepts.

The theoretical guarantees (Theorem 4.1) rest on strong, largely untestable assumptions (sufficiency, principal alignment, bounded leakage). The paper's own appendix shows these assumptions are violated under a plausible alternative SAE architecture (JumpReLU), invalidating both the guarantees and the evaluation itself, indicating the framework is fragile and highly dependent on unverifiable representation-learning properties in practice.

The authors explicitly acknowledge that, absent identifiability, the tool can only serve as a 'rescue system for hypotheses that may have been missed,' a much weaker claim than the paper's framing of discovering 'unknown effects... directly from data' as a general empiricist paradigm shift.

The semi-synthetic benchmark, while extensively ablated, is a fairly toy construction (only r=2 synthetic effects grafted onto CelebA attributes via a hand-designed DGP). Even in this favorable, fully-controlled setting, NES's absolute Precision is often well below 1 across many regimes, suggesting non-trivial residual false discovery even under best-case theoretical conditions.

The method depends critically on carefully choosing SAE hyperparameters and training regime, with no principled, unsupervised way to verify a priori whether the required assumptions hold in a new, genuinely unlabeled dataset, undermining practical applicability for real exploratory settings.

The additional CFL-inspired baselines (LASSO variants) provide only a modest point of comparison; no strong, established alternative from the heterogeneous treatment effect or causal representation learning literature is included, limiting the strength of the comparative evaluation.

Scope is narrow: binary treatment only, discrete/binary outcomes only, and a single real-world case study from one narrow domain, limiting the generalizability of the broad claims made about exploratory science at scale.

strengths: Novel problem formulation bridging causal inference, foundation models, and sparse autoencoders for exploratory (unsupervised) hypothesis generation in RCTs, addressing a genuine gap between rationalist and empiricist approaches to scientific discovery.

Strong theoretical contribution: the 'Paradox of Exploratory Causal Inference' is rigorously formalized and proven (Theorems 3.1-3.2), clearly demonstrating why naive multiple testing fails on entangled neural representations regardless of correction method.

Neural Effect Search (NES) algorithm is theoretically grounded, with a detailed consistency proof (Theorem 4.1) under explicit, clearly stated assumptions (sufficiency, alignment, arm-wise decomposition with bounded leakage).

Extensive and rigorous empirical validation: semi-synthetic CelebA experiments with known ground truth, plus a real-world ecological RCT (ISTAnt) showing the method recovers a scientifically validated behavior (grooming) as well as an interpretable finite-sample confound (background marking), illustrating practical value beyond simple effect recovery.

Very thorough appendix ablations covering different foundation models, SAE dimensions/non-linearities, random seeds, hypothesis-testing variants, residualization, ATE estimators, and structural causal model variations, substantially strengthening confidence in the robustness of the main claims.

Good positioning relative to related work (heterogeneous treatment effects, causal feature learning, causal representation learning, SAE interpretability), clearly explaining why prior methods do not solve the exploratory outcome-discovery problem.
Reasonable reproducibility: minimal Python implementation snippet, detailed training/evaluation protocols, and use of public datasets.

Honest and detailed limitations/ethics discussion, including explicit acknowledgment that SAE identifiability is not guaranteed and that the method should be used as a complement to (not replacement for) rationalist hypothesis testing.
weaknesses: The real-world validation is a single case study with a very small sample size (n=44 videos), and success is assessed largely qualitatively/via F1 against post-hoc biologist labels rather than through a rigorous, pre-registered quantitative causal validation; the claim of being the 'first successful' unsupervised causal discovery on a real trial is strong given this limited evidence.

The method's validity rests on several strong, largely untestable assumptions (FM sufficiency, principal neuron alignment, bounded leakage/disentanglement) that the authors' own ablations show can be violated in practice (e.g., JumpReLU SAEs break principal alignment for one of two concepts), raising concerns about robustness when ground truth is unavailable for verification.

The two novel 'Causal Feature Learning'-inspired baselines (LASSO/stability selection) are somewhat ad hoc/heuristic and not derived from a comparable theoretical framework, making the empirical comparison less balanced; no strong causal representation learning baselines are empirically compared despite being discussed at length in related work.

The paper's scope is restricted to discrete/binary outcomes, explicitly excluding continuous effects due to unresolved SAE interpretability issues for continuous concepts, which limits applicability to many real scientific settings.

The heavy theoretical apparatus (multiple assumptions, lengthy proofs) and dense notation may hinder accessibility and adoption; practical guidance on how to verify assumptions without ground-truth labels (as available only in semi-synthetic settings) is limited.
Efficiency/scalability of the recursive NES procedure (e.g., computational cost of repeated stratified testing over thousands of SAE codes) is not discussed or benchmarked.
